subtype: Stage 6: Scheduled closeness and honest limits [Response]
passage: Their Johannesburg calendar now had a new line in green: Wednesday, 8 pm, walk to the park, phones at home. Lucia had written it; Thabo had drawn a small tree beside it. The first Wednesday felt a bit forced. By the third, they were laughing about his mother's long voice notes all the way round the pond. The other rule got tested on Friday. Thabo came in grey-faced after a double shift. The old Thabo would have gone silent and let her wonder. Instead he said, "I'm spent. Give me an hour, then I'm yours." Lucia nodded. She didn't chase him down the corridor. She knew exactly when he'd be back, and he knew he wasn't letting her down by resting. At nine, he came to find her.

qa.q: What was written in green on the calendar?
qa.a: Wednesday, 8 pm, walk to the park, phones at home.

qa.q: Why could Lucia let Thabo rest without chasing him?
qa.a: She felt secure because she knew exactly when he would be back, so his rest no longer felt like being shut out.

qa.q: Which two agreements make this work?
qa.a: A regular, unhurried Wednesday walk without phones, and a clear line Thabo can use to ask for an hour before coming back.

qa.q: How does Thabo experience resting after the double shift now?
qa.a: He can rest without guilt, knowing he isn't letting Lucia down, because he has said when he will return.

grounding: Shows a couple with a regular unhurried time together and a clear phrase for his need for space, giving her predictability and him rest without guilt.

subtype: Stage 6: Scheduled closeness and honest limits [Response]
passage: At the community centre's Thursday couples' group, Rajni, the facilitator, asked each pair to share one thing that had changed. Jasleen went first, smiling a little. "Sundays, ten to twelve, are ours now. No phones, no in-laws. Just breakfast and a long walk." Manvir nodded. "And I've got a sentence I'm allowed to use." He glanced at Jasleen. "When I come off a night shift at the depot, I say, 'I'm spent, give me an hour, then I'm yours.'" "And he comes back," Jasleen said. "Every time so far. So I don't sit there spinning stories." Manvir rubbed his neck. "And I don't feel like a criminal for needing the hour." Rajni wrote both sentences on the whiteboard.

qa.q: Which hours on Sunday are theirs now?
qa.a: Sundays, ten to twelve, are theirs now.

qa.q: How has Manvir's feeling about needing rest changed?
qa.a: He feels less guilty now; he no longer feels like a criminal for needing the hour, because the break is agreed and he comes back.

qa.q: Why might Rajni write both sentences on the whiteboard?
qa.a: They give the group a practical model: a fixed, protected time together and an honest, clear way to ask for space.

qa.q: What difference does the promised return make to Jasleen?
qa.a: She no longer sits there spinning stories; knowing Manvir will come back gives her the predictability she needed.

grounding: Shows a couple describing a protected weekly time together and his agreed phrase for asking for an hour, easing her worry and his guilt.
